## Purpose

Works through the analyses still open on the paper roadmap:

1.  Re-score the assignment methods on informal messages only.
2.  Put uncertainty on the differences between methods.
3.  Cross-validate the methods whose tones are chosen from the data.
4.  Estimate honest best-case and worst-case benchmarks (how much headroom is real).
5.  Test preference reliability within person.
6.  Express method differences as effect sizes.
7.  Open items that need data or variables not in `panel.csv` (stubs at the end).

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: Setup
# Load packages and this study's functions, then read the cleaned panel in long format
# (one row per message rating). The seed makes the cross-validation folds and bootstrap
# resamples repeatable.
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)

source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/main/format_path.R")
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_llmpanel.R"))

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")

panel_long <- format_eda(read_csv(
  here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE), long = TRUE)

# tone_levels and pref_cols are defined in functions_llmpanel.R

set.seed(102030)
```

*Respondent-level tone means, pooled across styles and informal only*

```{r}
#| label: Tone Means
# Pooled across formal and informal (6 messages per tone), as in
# methods_first_round.qmd
tone_means <- panel_long |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, tone))

# Informal messages only (3 messages per tone)
tone_means_inf <- panel_long |>
  filter(style == "informal") |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, tone))

# Each respondent's preference score for each tone
pref_by_tone <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, across(all_of(pref_cols))) |>
  pivot_longer(-subid, names_to = "tone", names_prefix = "pref_", values_to = "pref")

# Sanity checks: one row per respondent and tone
stopifnot(nrow(tone_means) == n_distinct(tone_means$subid) * 5,
          nrow(tone_means_inf) == n_distinct(tone_means_inf$subid) * 5,
          nrow(pref_by_tone) == n_distinct(pref_by_tone$subid) * 5)
```

## Core Methods

One function scores a fixed set of core methods on any set of tone ratings, so
the pooled and informal-only versions are built the same way. Tones for the
mean-only, top-two and top-three methods are chosen from the sample means of
the ratings passed in.

```{r}
#| label: Core Method Function
# Returns a list with
#   tracker: one row per method (mean, sd, weighted_opt, weighted_dis)
#   ratings: one row per respondent and method (subid, method, rating)
#   tones:   the tones ranked by sample mean
score_core_methods <- function(tone_ratings, prefs) {
  ids <- unique(tone_ratings$subid)
  ranked <- tone_ratings |>
    summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating), .by = tone) |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rating))
  top <- ranked$tone

  fixed <- function(tones, weights = rep(1, length(tones))) {
    expand_grid(subid = ids, tibble(tone = tones, weight = weights))
  }

  methods <- list(
    "Uniform (all five)" = fixed(tone_levels),
    "Top three, equal" = fixed(top[1:3]),
    "Top three, 40/40/20" = fixed(top[1:3], c(.4, .4, .2)),
    "Top two, equal" = fixed(top[1:2]),
    "Mean-only" = fixed(top[1]),
    "Drop own two least-preferred" = drop_least_preferred(prefs, n_drop = 2) |>
      mutate(weight = 1),
    "Rule-based" = data_driven_weights(prefs) |> select(subid, tone, weight))

  scored <- imap(methods, \(w, nm) {
    m <- weighted_method(w, label = nm, tone_ratings = tone_ratings)
    list(
      row = track_method(NULL, m, weights = w, name = nm, tone_ratings = tone_ratings),
      ratings = m |> transmute(subid, method = nm, rating = weighted_rating))
  })

  # Benchmarks: each respondent's own highest- and lowest-rated tone
  bench <- tone_ratings |>
    summarise(`Best case` = max(rating), `Worst case` = min(rating), .by = subid) |>
    pivot_longer(-subid, names_to = "method", values_to = "rating")

  list(
    tracker = map(scored, "row") |> list_rbind() |>
      bind_rows(bench |> summarise(mean = mean(rating), sd = sd(rating), .by = method)) |>
      arrange(mean),
    ratings = map(scored, "ratings") |> list_rbind() |> bind_rows(bench),
    tones = ranked)
}
```

# 1. Informal-Only Re-Scoring

The paper recommends dropping formal messages, but the method comparison pools
both styles. Among informal messages value affirmation and self efficacy were
level, so the leading tone and the method ranking may change.

```{r}
#| label: Pooled vs Informal
core_pooled <- score_core_methods(tone_means, pref_by_tone)
core_inf <- score_core_methods(tone_means_inf, pref_by_tone)

# Tone order under each scoring
core_pooled$tones
core_inf$tones

# Side by side
full_join(
  core_pooled$tracker |> rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_pooled"), -method),
  core_inf$tracker |> rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_informal"), -method),
  by = "method") |>
  select(method, starts_with("mean"), starts_with("weighted_opt"),
         starts_with("weighted_dis")) |>
  arrange(mean_informal)
```

Note: the rule-based method's rules name self efficacy and value affirmation
directly. If the informal-only tone order differs, revisit the rules.

The rest of this script uses informal-only ratings. Switch here to compare.

```{r}
#| label: Choose Ratings
tone_ratings_use <- tone_means_inf
core <- core_inf
```

# 2. Uncertainty on Method Differences

Differences between methods are a few hundredths of a point. Every respondent
is scored under every method, so differences are paired. A respondent-level
bootstrap gives a 95% interval for each method's mean and for its difference
from the mean-only method.

```{r}
#| label: Bootstrap
n_boot <- 2000
reference <- "Mean-only"

ratings_wide <- core$ratings |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = rating) |>
  drop_na()
rating_mat <- as.matrix(select(ratings_wide, -subid))

boot_means <- map(seq_len(n_boot), \(i) {
  idx <- sample(nrow(rating_mat), replace = TRUE)
  colMeans(rating_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE])
}) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)

boot_summary <- tibble(
  method = colnames(rating_mat),
  mean = colMeans(rating_mat),
  mean_low = apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, .025),
  mean_high = apply(boot_means, 2, quantile, .975),
  diff_vs_ref = colMeans(rating_mat) - mean(rating_mat[, reference]),
  diff_low = apply(boot_means - boot_means[, reference], 2, quantile, .025),
  diff_high = apply(boot_means - boot_means[, reference], 2, quantile, .975)) |>
  arrange(mean)
boot_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: Bootstrap Plot
# Forest plot: each method's mean difference from the reference method, with its 95%
# bootstrap interval. The best-case and worst-case benchmarks are left out.
boot_summary |>
  filter(!method %in% c("Best case", "Worst case", reference)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_vs_ref, y = fct_reorder(method, diff_vs_ref))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = diff_low, xmax = diff_high)) +
  labs(x = paste0("Difference in mean helpfulness vs. ", reference,
                  " (95% bootstrap interval)"),
       y = NULL)
```

# 3. Cross-Validation of Data-Chosen Methods

The mean-only, top-two and top-three methods choose their tones from the same
ratings they are scored on. Here the tones are chosen in training folds and
scored on held-out respondents (6 repeats of 5-fold, matching the model's
outer loop). A small drop from the in-sample value means little optimism.

The rule-based method's rules were also written after looking at these data.
Its rules are fixed, so cross-validation cannot test them; a new sample would.

```{r}
#| label: Cross-Validation
n_repeats <- 6
n_folds <- 5
ids <- unique(tone_ratings_use$subid)

cv_results <- map(seq_len(n_repeats), \(r) {
  fold_id <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = length(ids)))
  map(seq_len(n_folds), \(k) {
    test_ids <- ids[fold_id == k]
    train <- tone_ratings_use |> filter(!subid %in% test_ids)
    test <- tone_ratings_use |> filter(subid %in% test_ids)

    top <- train |>
      summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating), .by = tone) |>
      arrange(desc(mean_rating)) |>
      pull(tone)

    score <- function(tones, weights = rep(1, length(tones))) {
      test |>
        inner_join(tibble(tone = tones, weight = weights), by = "tone") |>
        summarise(rating = sum(weight * rating) / sum(weight), .by = subid) |>
        pull(rating) |>
        mean()
    }

    tibble(
      rep = r, fold = k, top_tone = top[1],
      `Mean-only` = score(top[1]),
      `Top two, equal` = score(top[1:2]),
      `Top three, equal` = score(top[1:3]),
      `Top three, 40/40/20` = score(top[1:3], c(.4, .4, .2)),
      `Uniform (all five)` = score(tone_levels))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()

# How stable is the choice of the single best tone across training folds?
cv_results |> count(top_tone)

# Held-out vs. in-sample means
cv_results |>
  pivot_longer(-c(rep, fold, top_tone), names_to = "method", values_to = "held_out") |>
  summarise(held_out_mean = mean(held_out), held_out_sd = sd(held_out), .by = method) |>
  left_join(core$tracker |> select(method, in_sample_mean = mean), by = "method") |>
  mutate(optimism = in_sample_mean - held_out_mean)
```

# 4. Honest Benchmarks (How Much Headroom Is Real?)

The best-case benchmark picks each respondent's highest-rated tone and scores
it on the same ratings, so part of its advantage is noise. Here the best and
worst tones are picked from two risk contexts and scored on the third, for
each of the three contexts in turn. The gap that survives is the headroom an
ideal assignment could actually reach.

```{r}
#| label: Honest Benchmarks
context_means <- panel_long |>
  filter(style == "informal") |>          # remove this line for pooled styles
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, context, tone))

honest <- map(unique(context_means$context), \(held) {
  picked <- context_means |>
    filter(context != held) |>
    summarise(train_rating = mean(rating), .by = c(subid, tone)) |>
    mutate(is_best = near(train_rating, max(train_rating)),
           is_worst = near(train_rating, min(train_rating)),
           .by = subid)

  # Sample-level best tone from the same two contexts (mean-only, chosen blind)
  sample_top <- picked |>
    summarise(m = mean(train_rating), .by = tone) |>
    slice_max(m, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    pull(tone)

  picked |>
    inner_join(context_means |> filter(context == held) |>
                 select(subid, tone, test_rating = rating),
               by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
    summarise(
      best_case = mean(test_rating[is_best]),    # ties averaged
      worst_case = mean(test_rating[is_worst]),
      uniform = mean(test_rating),
      mean_only = mean(test_rating[tone == sample_top]),
      .by = subid) |>
    mutate(held_out = held)
}) |> list_rbind()

# By held-out context, then averaged
honest |>
  summarise(across(c(worst_case, uniform, mean_only, best_case), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            n = n(), .by = held_out)

honest_summary <- honest |>
  summarise(across(c(worst_case, uniform, mean_only, best_case), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .by = subid) |>
  summarise(across(-subid, \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
honest_summary

# Honest headroom above mean-only vs. the in-sample figure
honest_summary$best_case - honest_summary$mean_only
core$tracker |>
  filter(method %in% c("Best case", "Mean-only")) |>
  summarise(in_sample_headroom = max(mean) - min(mean))
```

Caveat: with informal-only ratings each context-by-tone cell is a single
message, so these picks are noisy. If the honest best case falls close to
mean-only, most of the in-sample headroom was noise. If it stays well above,
individuals have stable tone tastes that a method could learn.

# 6. Effect Sizes

Two ways to say whether a difference of 0.1 to 0.25 points matters: the
difference in SD units of respondent-level means, and the share of respondents
whose expected rating reaches "agree" (6) or "somewhat agree" (5).

```{r}
#| label: Effect Sizes
sd_uniform <- core$ratings |>
  filter(method == "Uniform (all five)") |>
  pull(rating) |>
  sd()

core$ratings |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating),
            pct_at_least_5 = mean(rating >= 5),
            pct_at_least_6 = mean(rating >= 6),
            .by = method) |>
  mutate(d_vs_uniform = (mean - mean[method == "Uniform (all five)"]) / sd_uniform) |>
  arrange(mean)
```

Paired effect size (Cohen's dz) for each method against mean-only:

```{r}
#| label: Paired Effect Sizes
ratings_wide |>
  pivot_longer(-c(subid, all_of(reference)), names_to = "method", values_to = "rating") |>
  mutate(diff = rating - .data[[reference]]) |>
  summarise(mean_diff = mean(diff), dz = mean(diff) / sd(diff), .by = method) |>
  arrange(mean_diff)
```

suggests excluded respondents rated messages uniformly high. To confirm,
